## Big Idea

Now that we have the [additive model](02AdditiveModel.qmd), we can put it to use. The model says a ring width is a sum of parts: the age trend, the climate, disturbance and noise. Pick a size and a shape for each part, add them up, and you have grown a tree on the computer. Do that for a stand and you have a collection where every part of every ring is known. This chapter builds one: 40 simulated tree-ring series, two cores from each of 20 trees in one stand. I wrote the code that made them, so I know every part of every ring. I also hid a few things in them. One core is missing a ring. Half the trees have neighbors crowding them, so their growth trends wander. One tree was released when a neighbor fell. And in one year, something knocked back half the trees standing at the time. None of it jumps out of the ring widths. This chapter shows how the stand is put together, and the later chapters go looking for each of those things with the method that is meant to find it.

A simulation lets you test each method: here is what went in, did it come back out, and if not, what got lost? Working with simulated data is a great way to learn how analytic methods behave. When you know the answer going in, every result is a check on the method, and the fun is in trying to get the answer back. I have been doing this for more than twenty years with tree-ring data and still find it useful [@Bunn2004].

- The opening now carries over from the model chapter (Andy, 2026-11-04). A question could still pull the reader in after it: here is a stand with four things hidden in it, so how would you know they are there?
- Promise: by the end you know how the stand is built, what is hidden where, and what the simulation leaves out.
